knowledge_point.title: Transforming First-Order Linear ODEs Using Integrating Factors

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\left(x\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(x\right)\cdot y=x^{4}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.

Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we write the equation in standard form. This gives

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y=x^{3}.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=1$ and $Q(x)=x^{3}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(1\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=e^{x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(e^{x}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}+y\right) & =\left(e^{x}\right)\cdot \left(x^{3}\right) \\ \left(e^{x}\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(1\right)\cdot \left(e^{x}\right)\cdot y & =\left(e^{x}\right)\cdot \left(x^{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(e^{x}\right)\right) & =\left(e^{x}\right)\cdot \left(x^{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Transforming First-Order Linear ODEs Using Integrating Factors

question.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y=y(x):$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\cdot y=x
$$

Write the equation in the form $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(yI(x))=I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
question.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x)
$$

with $P(x)=\frac{2}{3}$ and $Q(x)=x.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =e^{\int P(x)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\int \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\,dx} \\  & =e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x)=e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\cdot y\right) & =\left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(x\right) \\ \left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)\cdot \left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\cdot y & =\left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y\cdot I(x)):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\cdot \left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\right) & =\left(e^{\frac{2 x}{3}}\right)\cdot \left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$
